subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 11! In earlier units you learned what a fraction is and how to name simple fractions like one half and one quarter. Now you will take a big step forward. You will learn how to find equivalent fractions, how to compare and order fractions that have different denominators, and for the very first time you will meet percentages. You will also see how fractions, decimals and percentages are really three different ways of describing the very same amount.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 4 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Identify and generate equivalent fractions using diagrams and by multiplying or dividing.
Compare and order fractions, including fractions with different denominators.
Understand that a percentage means ‘out of 100’ and use the % symbol.
Convert between fractions and percentages for common values.
Work with tenths and hundredths and link them to percentages.
See how fractions, decimals and percentages describe the same amount.
Find a percentage of an amount and find the whole when you know a percentage.
Solve word problems involving fractions and percentages in real-life situations.

concepts.title: Equivalent Fractions
concepts.explanation:
Equivalent fractions are fractions that have the same value, even though they may look different. For example, 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent because they represent exactly the same amount. Think of it like cutting a mango. Whether you cut the mango into 2 equal pieces and take 1 piece, or cut the same mango into 4 equal pieces and take 2 pieces, you end up with the same amount of mango in your hand.

We can picture this with a bar split into parts. When a bar is cut in half and one half is shaded, exactly the same amount is coloured as when the bar is cut into four and two parts are shaded, or cut into eight and four parts are shaded. So 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. They all fill the same length of the bar.

There is a neat rule for making equivalent fractions without drawing anything. If you multiply (or divide) the numerator and the denominator by the same number, the value of the fraction does not change. Watch what happens to 1/2:

1/2 with top and bottom × 2 gives 2/4.

1/2 with top and bottom × 4 gives 4/8.

1/2 with top and bottom × 5 gives 5/10.

Going the other way, 6/8 with top and bottom ÷ 2 gives 3/4.

The important word is same – you must multiply or divide the top and the bottom by the *same* number. If you multiply only the top, or only the bottom, you change the value and the fractions are no longer equivalent. When you divide the top and bottom to make the numbers smaller, we say you are simplifying the fraction. The simplest form of a fraction is the one with the smallest whole numbers, like 3/4 instead of 6/8.

Here is a useful skill: filling in a missing number to complete an equivalent fraction. Suppose you must complete 3/4 = ?/12. Ask yourself: what did the denominator do to change 4 into 12? It was multiplied by 3, because 4 × 3 = 12. So you must do the same to the numerator: 3 × 3 = 9. Therefore 3/4 = 9/12. Always find the link between the two denominators first, then apply the very same change to the numerator.

Why does this rule work? When you multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the same number, you are simply cutting each piece of the whole into more, smaller pieces – but you keep the same amount coloured in. Imagine an anjero cut into 2 halves with 1 half on your plate. If you now cut every piece in two, you have 4 quarters and 2 of them on your plate. Your plate holds exactly the same amount of anjero; you have only changed how many cuts you made. That is why 1/2 and 2/4 are equal. Nothing was added or taken away – only the number of pieces changed.
concepts.example: You can also spot equivalent fractions on a number line. Draw a line from 0 to 1. If you mark the halfway point, that is 1/2. If you split the same line into 4 equal steps, the second step lands on exactly the same spot, and that is 2/4. Because 1/2 and 2/4 sit at the very same point on the line, they must be equal. A number line is a good way to *check* whether two fractions are equivalent: if they land on the same point, they are equivalent; if not, they are not.

concepts.title: Comparing and Ordering Fractions
concepts.explanation:
To compare two fractions means to decide which is larger, which is smaller, or whether they are equal. When two fractions have the same denominator, comparing is easy: the fraction with the larger numerator is the larger fraction. This makes sense, because the parts are the same size, so more parts means more of the whole.

3/8 < 5/8 because 3 parts is fewer than 5 parts of the same size.

7/10 > 3/10 because 7 tenths is more than 3 tenths.

When the denominators are different, you cannot compare the numerators directly, because the parts are different sizes. First you must rewrite the fractions so they share a common denominator. Here are the steps:

Find a common denominator (a number both denominators divide into).

Change each fraction into an equivalent fraction with that denominator.

Example: compare 3/4 and 5/8. A good common denominator is 8, because 4 divides into 8. Change 3/4 into eighths: 3/4 = (3 × 2)/(4 × 2) = 6/8. Now compare 6/8 and 5/8. Since 6 > 5, we know 6/8 > 5/8, and therefore 3/4 > 5/8. Notice how turning the fractions into the same family of eighths made the comparison simple.

Ordering fractions means putting a whole set of them in order, usually from smallest to largest. The method is the same: change them all to a common denominator, then order them by their numerators. Example: order 1/2, 3/8 and 3/4 from smallest to largest. Use 8 as the common denominator: 1/2 = 4/8, 3/8 stays as 3/8, and 3/4 = 6/8. Now order the eighths: 3/8, 4/8, 6/8. So the fractions in order are 3/8, 1/2, 3/4.
concepts.example: A common trap catches many learners here. A fraction is not larger just because its denominator is larger. In fact, when the numerator is 1, a larger denominator makes a smaller fraction, because you are splitting the whole into more, tinier pieces. So 1/8 is smaller than 1/4, even though 8 is bigger than 4. If you share one anjero between 8 people, each piece is smaller than if you share it between 4 people. Always think about the size of the pieces, not just the size of the numbers.

concepts.title: What a Percentage Means
concepts.explanation:
A percentage is a special way of writing a fraction whose denominator is 100. The word percent comes from words meaning ‘per hundred’, and the symbol we use is %. So a percentage always answers the question: how many out of every hundred? This is the single most important idea in the whole unit, so let us say it clearly: a percentage is a number of parts out of 100.

25% means 25 out of 100, which is the fraction 25/100.

50% means 50 out of 100, which is 50/100.

75% means 75 out of 100, which is 75/100.

100% means 100 out of 100 – the whole thing.

A wonderful way to picture percentages is a 10 × 10 grid. The grid has 100 small squares altogether, so the whole grid is 100%. If you shade 25 of the squares, you have shaded 25%. If you shade 50 squares, that is 50%, exactly half the grid. If you shade 75 squares, that is 75%. Because the grid always has 100 squares, the number of shaded squares is the percentage. Drawing and shading these grids is one of the best ways to feel what a percentage really is.

Percentages appear all around you in daily life. In shops you see discounts like ‘20% off’. On devices you see battery levels like ‘85% charged’. On tests you see scores like ‘90% correct’. In weather forecasts you hear ‘30% chance of rain’. On food labels you read ‘15% of your daily needs’. Each of these is a way of saying ‘this many out of every hundred’. Because everything is measured against the same 100, percentages make it easy to compare very different things fairly.
concepts.example: Why are percentages so useful? Imagine Omar took a test with 20 questions and got 18 right, while Zahra took a different test with 50 questions and got 44 right. Who did better? It is hard to tell just by looking, because the tests had different numbers of questions. But if we turn each score into a percentage – a score out of 100 – we can compare them fairly. Omar scored 90% and Zahra scored 88%, so Omar did a little better. This is the real power of percentages: they put everything onto the same scale of 100 so that fair comparison becomes easy. That is exactly why shops, schools, doctors and scientists all reach for percentages.

concepts.title: Converting Between Fractions and Percentages
concepts.explanation:
Because a percentage is just a fraction out of 100, changing between the two forms is all about the number 100. To change a fraction into a percentage, rewrite it as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100. The new numerator is the percentage.

Example: change 1/4 into a percentage. Ask what turns 4 into 100. The answer is 25, because 4 × 25 = 100. Do the same to the top: 1 × 25 = 25. So 1/4 = 25/100 = 25%. In the same way, 1/2 = 50/100 = 50%, and 3/4 = 75/100 = 75%.

Some fraction-to-percentage pairs come up so often that it is worth learning them by heart. Knowing these makes many problems quick:
concepts.example: To change a percentage into a fraction, write it over 100 and then simplify if you can. Example: change 75% into a fraction. Start with 75/100. Both numbers divide by 25: 75 ÷ 25 = 3 and 100 ÷ 25 = 4. So 75% = 3/4. Another example: 20% = 20/100, and dividing top and bottom by 20 gives 1/5. Always simplify to the smallest numbers so your fraction is in its simplest form.

concepts.title: Tenths, Hundredths, Decimals and Percentages
concepts.explanation:
Tenths and hundredths are special fractions that link beautifully to percentages. A tenth is one part out of ten equal parts (1/10). A hundredth is one part out of one hundred equal parts (1/100). Because percentages are all about hundredths, these fractions turn into percentages very easily.

To change a tenth into a percentage, multiply the top and bottom by 10 to get a denominator of 100. For example, 1/10 = 10/100 = 10%; 3/10 = 30/100 = 30%; and 7/10 = 70/100 = 70%. To change a hundredth into a percentage is even easier – the numerator is already out of 100, so it *is* the percentage: 1/100 = 1%, 27/100 = 27%, and 83/100 = 83%.

There is a third way to write these amounts: as a decimal. Fractions, decimals and percentages are simply three different costumes for the same value. For instance, one quarter can be dressed as the fraction 1/4, the decimal 0.25, or the percentage 25% – and all three mean exactly the same amount. Being able to move between the three forms is a powerful skill. This table shows the most useful links:
concepts.example: A good real-life picture of hundredths is money. Think of one shilling divided into 100 small parts. One small part is one hundredth of a shilling, which is 1%. Fifty of those parts is half the shilling, or 50%. This is why percentages feel so natural when we talk about money, sharing and measuring – they are built on the same idea of splitting a whole into a hundred equal pieces.

concepts.title: Finding a Percentage of an Amount
concepts.explanation:
Often we want to find a percentage of a real quantity – for example, 25% of the 20 children in a class. The safest way for now is to turn the percentage into a simple fraction, then find that fraction of the amount. Because you already know the common percentage-fraction pairs, this becomes straightforward.

Example: find 50% of 20. Since 50% = 1/2, we need half of 20, which is 10. Example: find 25% of 40. Since 25% = 1/4, we need a quarter of 40, which is 40 ÷ 4 = 10. Example: find 10% of 50. Since 10% = 1/10, we need one tenth of 50, which is 50 ÷ 10 = 5. Finding 10% by dividing by 10 is an especially handy trick, because once you know 10% you can build up other percentages.

You can also work backwards to find the whole when you know a percentage. Suppose 25% of a number is 12. Since 25% is one quarter, the number 12 is one quarter of the whole. So the whole is 12 × 4 = 48. Another example: if 10% of a number is 7, then because 10% is one tenth, the whole is 7 × 10 = 70. The idea is to figure out how many of the given parts make a full 100%, then multiply.

The 10% trick is worth practising until it becomes automatic, because it is the master key to percentages. Once you can find 10% of an amount by dividing by 10, you can build almost any other percentage. To find 20%, find 10% and double it. To find 5%, find 10% and halve it. To find 30%, find 10% and multiply by three. For example, to find 30% of 60 shillings: 10% of 60 is 6, so 30% is 3 × 6 = 18 shillings. Building percentages up from 10% in small, safe steps means you rarely have to guess, and you can check your answer makes sense at every stage.

It also helps to notice that some percentages are just benchmark amounts you already know from fractions. 50% is a half, so 50% of anything is simply half of it. 25% is a quarter, so you divide by 4. 100% is the whole thing, and 0% is nothing at all. If a problem asks for 50% of 46, you do not need any clever method – you just halve 46 to get 23. Spotting these friendly benchmarks first can save you a lot of work.

You have now met six big ideas: equivalent fractions, comparing and ordering fractions, what a percentage means, converting between fractions and percentages, tenths and hundredths linked to decimals, and finding percentages of amounts. These ideas are not separate islands – they work together. Equivalent fractions are the key that unlocks comparing fractions *and* converting to percentages, because both rely on rewriting a fraction with a new denominator.

When Khadija sees a shirt with ‘20% off’ at the Mombasa market, she uses several ideas at once. She knows 20% means 20/100, which simplifies to 1/5. She finds one fifth of the price to get the discount, then subtracts it to find the sale price. In a single everyday moment she is using percentages, equivalent fractions and finding a fraction of an amount – exactly the skills in this unit. The more you practise, the more these ideas join up into quick, confident thinking.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into your memory is to use them with real things around you. Shade grids to see percentages. Fold paper to see equivalent fractions. Look for percentages on food labels and shop signs. Every time you do this, your number sense grows a little stronger, and the harder maths in later units will feel much easier. Now let us practise together with some worked examples.

methods.title: How to make an equivalent fraction
steps: Decide the new denominator you want.
Work out what the old denominator was multiplied (or divided) by.
Do exactly the same to the numerator.
Write the new equivalent fraction.

methods.title: How to compare fractions with different denominators
steps: Find a common denominator both numbers divide into.
Change each fraction to that denominator.
Compare the numerators.
Write the correct symbol: <, > or =.

methods.title: How to change a fraction into a percentage
steps: Make an equivalent fraction with denominator 100.
The new numerator is the percentage.

methods.title: Order three fractions
methods.example: Order 1/2, 3/8 and 5/8 from smallest to largest.
steps: Solution: Use 8 as the common denominator.
1/2 = 4/8, and the others are already eighths.
In eighths: 3/8, 4/8, 5/8.
So the order is 3/8, 1/2, 5/8.

methods.title: Fraction to percentage
steps: Solution: What turns 5 into 100?
It is × 20, because 5 × 20 = 100.
Do the same to the top: 3 × 20 = 60.

methods.title: Percentage to fraction
methods.example: Change 35% into a fraction in its simplest form.
steps: Solution: Write it over 100: 35/100.
Both divide by 5: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 and 100 ÷ 5 = 20.
Nothing bigger than 1 divides both 7 and 20, so this is simplest form.

workedExamples.title: Make an equivalent fraction
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Look at the denominators. What turns 3 into 12? It is × 4, because 3 × 4 = 12. Do the same to the numerator: 2 × 4 = 8. So 2/3 = 8/12.

workedExamples.title: Simplify a fraction
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Find a number that divides both 6 and 8. Both divide by 2. So 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, giving 3/4. No number bigger than 1 divides both 3 and 4, so 3/4 is the simplest form.

workedExamples.title: Compare fractions with different denominators
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Use a common denominator of 12. Change both: 3/4 = 9/12 and 2/3 = 8/12. Now compare: 9/12 > 8/12, so 3/4 > 2/3.

workedExamples.title: Order three fractions
workedExamples.prompt: Order 1/2, 3/8 and 5/8 from smallest to largest.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Use 8 as the common denominator. 1/2 = 4/8, and the others are already eighths. In eighths: 3/8, 4/8, 5/8. So the order is 3/8, 1/2, 5/8.

workedExamples.title: Fraction to percentage
workedExamples.solution: Solution: What turns 5 into 100? It is × 20, because 5 × 20 = 100. Do the same to the top: 3 × 20 = 60. So 3/5 = 60/100 = 60%.

workedExamples.title: Percentage to fraction
workedExamples.prompt: Change 35% into a fraction in its simplest form.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Write it over 100: 35/100. Both divide by 5: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 and 100 ÷ 5 = 20. So 35% = 7/20. Nothing bigger than 1 divides both 7 and 20, so this is simplest form.

workedExamples.title: Find a percentage of an amount
workedExamples.solution: Solution: 75% = 3/4. Find one quarter of 20 first: 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Then three quarters is 3 × 5 = 15. So 75% of 20 is 15.

workedExamples.title: A shopping percentage problem
workedExamples.prompt: A shirt costs 25 shillings. In a sale it is reduced by 20%. What is the sale price?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: First find 20% of 25. Since 20% = 1/5, one fifth of 25 is 25 ÷ 5 = 5 shillings off. Now subtract: 25 − 5 = 20 shillings. The sale price is 20 shillings.

workedExamples.title: Find the whole from a percentage
workedExamples.prompt: If 30% of a number is 15, what is the number?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: First find 10% by dividing 30% (which is 15) by 3: 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so 10% is 5. The whole is 100%, which is ten lots of 10%: 5 × 10 = 50. So the number is 50.

workedExamples.title: A test score as a percentage
workedExamples.prompt: Aisha scored 16 out of 20 in a spelling test. What is her score as a percentage?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Her score is the fraction 16/20. To turn it into a percentage, make an equivalent fraction out of 100. What turns 20 into 100? It is × 5, because 20 × 5 = 100. Do the same to the top: 16 × 5 = 80. So 16/20 = 80/100 = 80%. Aisha scored 80%.

workedExamples.title: A missing percentage
workedExamples.prompt: In a class, 40% of pupils chose football and 35% chose swimming. The rest chose running. What percentage chose running?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: The whole class is 100%. Add the two known parts: 40% + 35% = 75%. The rest is 100% − 75% = 25%. So 25% of the class chose running. Always check that all the percentages add up to 100%.

workedExamples.title: Find each amount
workedExamples.prompt: Find each amount: a) 50% of 20 b) 25% of 40 c) 10% of 50 d) 75% of 20.

activities.title: Paper-Folding Equivalent Fractions
activities.materials: a few sheets of paper and a pencil.
steps: Fold one sheet in half and shade one half. Write 1/2 on it.
Fold another identical sheet into quarters and shade two of them. Write 2/4.
Fold a third sheet into eighths and shade four. Write 4/8.
Line up the shaded parts. What do you notice? Write the equivalent fractions you have shown.
You have just proved with your own hands that 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8.

activities.title: Shade the 100-Square
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, and two coloured pencils.
steps: Draw a 10 × 10 grid so it has 100 small squares.
Shade 25 squares in one colour. What percentage is that? What fraction?
Shade another 25 squares in a second colour. Now what percentage is shaded in total?
Ask a family member to name a percentage and you shade the matching number of squares.

activities.title: Percentage Hunt Around the Home
activities.materials: food labels, shop receipts, a phone or radio.
steps: Find five percentages in real life (battery level, discount signs, food labels, test scores).
Write each percentage down and say what it means ‘out of 100’.
For each one, write the matching fraction in its simplest form.
Share your five finds with your teacher at the next session.

activities.title: The Market Discount Game
activities.materials: small stones or bottle caps as pretend shillings, and paper price tags.
steps: Set up a pretend market stall with items priced in tens (10, 20, 30, 40 shillings).
One player is the shopkeeper and calls out a discount like ‘20% off’.
The buyer works out the discount and the new price using coins.
Swap roles and play again with different prices and discounts.

activities.title: Fraction, Decimal and Percentage Snap
steps: Make cards showing values in three forms: some fractions (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/10), some decimals (0.5, 0.25, 0.75, 0.1), some percentages (50%, 25%, 75%, 10%).
Shuffle and deal the cards to two players.
Take turns laying a card down. Shout ‘Snap!’ when two cards show the same value in different forms.
The fastest player keeps the pair. Play until the cards run out.

activities.title: Investigation – Sharing Fairly
activities.materials: 20 small objects (dates, beans or stones) and some family members.
steps: Share 20 dates so that one person gets 50%, one gets 25% and one gets 25%. How many does each get?
Now try 20 dates shared as 10%, 40% and 50%. How many each?
Check that your percentages always add up to 100%.
Make up your own fair-sharing puzzle and give it to a friend to solve.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand equivalent fractions best? How did shading the 100-square help you picture percentages? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Equivalent Fractions Rule
rules.text: Multiply or divide the top and the bottom by the SAME number. 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. The value does not change.

rules.title: Comparing Fractions Rule
rules.text: Same denominator: the bigger numerator is the bigger fraction. Different denominators: make a common denominator first, then compare.

rules.title: Percentage Rule
rules.text: A percentage means a number out of 100. The symbol is %. 25% = 25 out of 100 = 25/100 = 1/4.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Find each amount: a) 50% of 20 b) 25% of 40 c) 10% of 50 d) 75% of 20.
Find the whole: a) 25% of a number is 12 b) 10% of a number is 7 c) 50% of a number is 35.
In a class of 30, 40% are boys. How many boys are there, and how many girls?
A book has 160 pages. You have read 75% of it. How many pages are left?
30% of pupils have blue eyes and 45% have brown eyes. The rest have green eyes. What percentage have green eyes?
Explain the key idea in Finding a Percentage of an Amount.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: To find a percentage of an amount, first change the percentage into a simple fraction (for example 25% = 1/4), then find that fraction of the amount. For example, to find 25% of 40, use one quarter of 40, which is 40 ÷ 4 = 10.

selfAssessment: I can identify and generate equivalent fractions using diagrams and by multiplying or dividing.
I can compare and order fractions, including fractions with different denominators.
I can understand that a percentage means ‘out of 100’ and use the % symbol.
I can convert between fractions and percentages for common values.
I can work with tenths and hundredths and link them to percentages.
I can see how fractions, decimals and percentages describe the same amount.
I can find a percentage of an amount and find the whole when you know a percentage.
I can solve word problems involving fractions and percentages in real-life situations.
